The bus had passed his stop. Then it began accelerating. Acie looked toward the front and saw the driver unconscious over the steering wheel. The moving bus, carrying 14 students, was drifting across the centerline toward oncoming traffic. Acie did not scream. He did not freeze. He did not wait for an adult to save them. This eighth grader ran forward, seized the steering wheel, guided the bus back into its lane, moved the driver’s foot from the accelerator and pressed the brake until that enormous bus came safely to the curb. He could not find the parking brake, so he turned the wheels hard toward the curb to prevent the bus from rolling away. That is presence of mind under pressure. Then Acie checked on the younger students, told them to contact their parents, made certain 911 had been called and went to get his grandmother, Phyllis Holland, who is a nurse. The driver regained consciousness and received medical care. Every student made it home safely. Acie had worked on cars with his father and enjoyed go-karting, but nothing could have completely prepared a 14-year-old boy to take control of a moving school bus. Something had already been built inside him: courage, mechanical understanding, responsibility and the instinct to protect others. His classmates gave him a new name: “AC-Hero.” That name fits. While the world spends enormous energy telling us what is wrong with young men, Acie Holland III reminded us what can be right with them. Fourteen students reached home because one young man recognized the danger, stepped forward and acted. May God continue to strengthen this remarkable young man. #AStoneGroove #SilentMajoritySpeaks

tweets.text: RT @lex_node: finally some actual arguments! I previously had to steelman my way into this one (https://t.co/lJ1ZYasTVg), flagging it as the strongest possible argument the tapered-issuance side has. The worry is real in theory: if a huge fraction of ETH ends up staked through a handful of large intermediaries (ETFs, DATs, exchanges), then slashing them starts to look like punishing a big slice of “involuntary” holders, and the social will to enforce the penalty (or to coordinate a rescue fork the other way) could evaporate. At that point the deterrence softens and censorship resistance weakens. Where I diverge is on urgency and side-effects: We’re still only ~34% staked. The scenario that makes social slashing non-credible sits much higher — I’d guess 60-80% before it becomes a real political problem, and even that is speculative. No one really knows at % staked the political argument against social slashing "tips" into social slashing being politically unfeasible--and the answer may differ depending on the particular social slashing scenario facts at issue in a given case. Whatever the 'bad level' is, if it's much higher than current, there is good reason to think we may never get there. Chains that offered far higher APRs and carried less real slashing or intermediation risk (Solana is the clearest example) still stabilized well below 70%. Ethereum already has meaningful slashing risk and a much lower base APR even under the current curve. Restaking was once expected to drive significantly higher participation and has not done so. Meanwhile, Ethereum has never executed a social slash, and pretty much no other major chain has either. If maintaining a credible threat of social slashing is the problem this proposal solves, it should be accompanied by a careful examination of when we would actually use it and whether a high overall staking ratio would truly deter it in those scenarios. The closest serious discussion (post-Tornado Cash OFAC sanctions) focused on the relative stake weight of a censoring majority, not the absolute percentage of ETH staked. Vitalik’s “Don’t overload Ethereum’s social consensus” essay (https://t.co/qQtpKnIvre) likewise does not treat total stake percentage as the key variable. People who use staking-as-a-service or delegation already accept that they can be impacted by operator faults. So there is at best speculative and theoretical upside to reducing stake weight in corner-case scenarios that have never happened. Meanwhile, changing the curve now carries much more likely and proximal risks. Most importantly, it risks making the centralization problem worse, not better. Large exchanges can cross-subsidize thin staking margins with other business lines, MEV, bundled products, etc. Pure liquid-staking protocols and solo stakers cannot. The participants most likely to exit first are the more decentralized ones, leaving a higher relative share controlled by the entities that are hardest to slash socially. That moves us toward the bad equilibrium faster, not slower. On top of that, the Ethereum roadmap still has major consensus-role changes coming (attester-includer separation and related work). Whatever issuance policy we land on will probably need to be revisited once those are live (see https://t.co/aGiRYJ6Ll6). Doing a significant monetary-policy intervention now, only to reopen the question a year or two later, feels premature. I’d rather treat high staking ratios as a symptom and attack the actual drivers of intermediation and concentration more directly, instead of using the issuance curve as a blunt preemptive instrument against a future that hasn’t arrived yet. Proposals more specifically aimed at social-slashing robustness, reducing intermediation, or supporting solo staking would make more sense — the stake ratio is at most a symptom of some of these issues, and simply disincentivizing staking in general will not solve them and is not even guaranteed to mitigate them. Happy to be wrong if the data starts showing the credibility of penalties actually eroding. Right now I just don’t see the urgency that justifies the downside risk to solo and decentralized stakers, or the disruption to the consistency and economic properties that institutions and DeFi builders currently rely on.
